title: Much (of), many (of), a lot of, lots (of), etc.

sections.title: Much (of), many (of), a lot of, lots (of)
sections.content:
In affirmative sentences we generally use a lot of and lots (of) rather than much (of) and many (of), particularly in informal contexts. However, there are a number of exceptions:
- In formal contexts, such as academic writing, much (of) and many (of) are preferred. We can also use phrases such as a large / considerable / substantial amount of (with uncountable nouns), or a large / considerable / great / substantial number of (with plural nouns):
• Much debate has been heard about Thornton's new book.
• The book contains a large number of pictures, many in colour. (or ... many ...)
- In formal contexts we can use much and many as pronouns:
• There is no guarantee she will recover. Much depends on how well she responds to treatment.
• Not once did I see a tiger in the jungle, although I heard many.
- We usually use many rather than a lot of or lots of with time expressions (days, minutes, months, weeks, years) and number + of:
• We used to spend many hours driving to Melbourne and back.

sections.title: many following the, my, its, etc.
sections.content:
We can use many following the, my, its, his, her, etc. and plural countable nouns:
• Among the many unknowns after the earthquake is the extent of the structural damage.
We can use the phrase many a with a singular noun to talk about a repeated event or a large number of people or things:
• Many a pupil at the school will be pleased that Latin is no longer compulsory.

sections.title: Emphasising large numbers or amounts
sections.content:
To emphasise a large number we can use a good / great many with a plural noun:
• She has a good / great many friends in New Zealand.
To emphasise a large amount we can use a good / great deal of with a singular or uncountable noun:
• A good / great deal of the exhibition was devoted to her recent work.

sections.title: far too many / much
sections.content:
We use far (not 'much' or 'many') before too many + a plural countable noun or too much + an uncountable noun:
• Far too many students failed the end-of-year maths exam. (not Much / Many too many ...)
• Far too much time is wasted filling in forms. (not Much / Many too much time ...)

sections.title: plenty of
sections.content:
We often use plenty of instead of a lot of or lots of with uncountable and plural countable nouns. However, plenty of means 'enough, or more than enough' and is therefore not always appropriate:
• We took lots of / plenty of food and drink on our walk through the hills.
• Nina doesn't look well. She's lost a lot of weight. ('plenty of' is unlikely here)

sections.title: Informal quantifiers
sections.content:
We can use quantifiers like millions of (+ a plural countable noun), loads of and tons of (+ uncountable or plural countable noun) in informal contexts, exaggerating to stress large numbers or quantities:
• I've got tons of work to do before I get away on holiday.
• There were millions of people out shopping today. It was unbearable.

exercises.question: While it is true that [a lot of] thousands of jobs were lost... What would be a better choice in academic writing?
exercises.hint: Use 'many' with number expressions like 'thousands of'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: many
Use 'many' with number expressions like 'thousands of'.

exercises.sentence: There are much people waiting outside in the queue.
exercises.correction: There are many people waiting outside in the queue.
acceptable: There are a lot of people
exercises.hint: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns; 'many' is used with countable nouns like 'people'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: There are many people waiting
'Much' is used with uncountable nouns (much water, much information, much time). 'Many' is used with countable nouns (many people, many cars, many opportunities). 'People' is countable (one person, two people), so 'many' is correct. 'A lot of / lots of' works with both: 'a lot of people', 'a lot of time'.

exercises.question: She went to stay in Munich with one of ___.
exercises.hint: We can use 'many' following possessives like 'her' and plural countable nouns.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: her many German relatives
We can use 'many' following possessives like 'her' and plural countable nouns. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.sentence: She doesn't have much friends in the new city yet.
exercises.correction: She doesn't have many friends in the new city yet.
acceptable: She doesn't have a lot of friends
exercises.hint: 'Friends' is countable — use 'many' not 'much' in negatives.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: She doesn't have many friends
In negative and question sentences, use 'many' with countable nouns and 'much' with uncountable nouns. 'Much' with countable nouns ('much friends', 'much cars') is always wrong. In positive sentences, 'a lot of' and 'lots of' are more natural than 'many' or 'much' in informal English.

exercises.question: I spent ___ sitting on the terrace looking out over the hills.
exercises.hint: Use 'many a' + singular noun to talk about a repeated event.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: many a sunny afternoon
Use 'many a' + singular noun to talk about a repeated event. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.sentence: We don't have much time, so let's not waste it discussing minor details.
exercises.correction: We don't have much time, so let's not waste it discussing minor details.
acceptable: We don't have much time, so let's not waste it discussing minor details.
exercises.hint: 'Time' is uncountable — 'much time' in a negative sentence is correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: We don't have much time — CORRECT
'Time' in this sense (duration, the abstract concept) is uncountable — 'much time' is correct. Compare: 'We don't have much time' (correct) vs 'There were many times when...' (countable — specific occasions). Context determines whether 'time' is countable (specific instances) or uncountable (duration/quantity).

exercises.question: Nina doesn't look well. She's lost ___ weight.
exercises.hint: 'Plenty of' means 'enough, or more than enough', which is unlikely here.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: a lot of
'Plenty of' means 'enough, or more than enough', which is unlikely here. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: We use ___ before 'too many' or 'too much' to emphasise the amount.
exercises.hint: We say 'far too many' and 'far too much'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: far
'Far' is used as an intensifier before 'too + adjective/adverb' to emphasise excess: 'far too late', 'far too many'. Other intensifiers in this pattern: 'rather too', 'somewhat too', 'much too'.
